goals: Decide whether a company must keep a Debenture Redemption Reserve and calculate the 10% minimum

slides.heading: Redemption of Debentures
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **reserve**, the **investment** and the **source** of the money. Every company and figure in this chapter is imagined.

nodes.label: Why debentures need planning for repayment
Debenture Redemption Reserve: who and how much
Debenture Redemption Investment: 15% by 30 April
Out of profits or out of capital

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why repayment of debentures must be planned, who must keep a debenture redemption reserve and how much, the fifteen per cent investment made by the thirtieth of April, and redemption out of profits or out of capital
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Debentures are borrowed money, and one day they must be repaid. Repaying them is called redemption. The law makes many companies prepare for that day in two ways: by keeping back profit in a reserve, and by setting money aside in a safe investment. In this part we learn who must do what, how much, and how the source of the repayment changes the entries.

slides.heading: Redemption: method, source and safeguards
bullets: **Method:** one lump sum at maturity, or instalments chosen by draw of lots.
**Source:** out of capital, or partly or wholly out of profits.

nodes.label: Redemption: repaying the debentureholders
Method: one lump sum at maturity, or instalments by draw of lots
Source: out of capital, or (partly or wholly) out of profits
Safeguards: Debenture Redemption Reserve and Debenture Redemption Investment

visual.alt: Flow of the ideas in redemption: redemption means repaying the debentureholders; the method is a lump sum at maturity or instalments by draw of lots; the source is capital or profits; the safeguards are the reserve and the investment
visual.caption: Redemption: method, source and safeguards

slides.narration: Three questions frame every redemption. How is the money repaid: all at once at maturity, or in instalments chosen by draw of lots? Where does it come from: out of capital, or out of profits kept back for the purpose? And what safeguards does the law demand: a debenture redemption reserve and a debenture redemption investment.

slides.heading: Who must keep a Debenture Redemption Reserve?
slides.body_md: Section 71(4) of the **Companies Act, 2013**, with Rule 18(7) as amended in 2019.

**15%** of debentures maturing in the year

visual.alt: Table of who must keep the reserve and the investment: All India Financial Institutions, banking companies and unlisted non-banking or housing finance companies with privately placed debentures need neither; listed companies need no reserve but must make the fifteen per cent investment; other unlisted companies need a ten per cent reserve and the fifteen per cent investment
visual.caption: Section 71(4): the reserve comes out of profits available for dividend and is used only for redemption.

slides.narration: The Companies Act says the reserve must be created out of profits available for dividend, and used only to redeem debentures. Since the amendment of twenty nineteen, only ordinary unlisted companies must keep it, at ten per cent of outstanding debentures. Listed companies, banks, financial institutions, and unlisted finance companies with privately placed debentures are spared the reserve.

slides.heading: The Debenture Redemption Investment
slides.body_md: A reserve keeps profit back; the **investment** actually sets **money** aside.

rows: Listed companies and other unlisted companies (not banks, All India Financial Institutions, or unlisted NBFCs and HFCs on private placement)
At least **15%** of the debentures **maturing during the year** ending on the next 31 March
On or before **30 April** of that year
Scheduled bank deposits free from charge or lien; unencumbered Central or State Government securities; unencumbered trust securities and notified bonds under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882
Only to redeem the debentures maturing that year; never below 15% of them

visual.alt: Table of the investment rule: listed and ordinary unlisted companies must invest at least fifteen per cent of the debentures maturing in the year, by the thirtieth of April, in bank deposits free from charge, government securities or trust securities, and use it only to redeem those debentures

slides.narration: A reserve is only a book entry, so the rules add a second safeguard. By the thirtieth of April each year, listed companies and ordinary unlisted companies must invest or deposit at least fifteen per cent of the debentures maturing during that year, in safe forms such as a bank deposit free from any charge, or government securities. The money may be used only to repay those debentures.

The unlisted company needs both: a reserve of rupees five lakh and an investment of rupees three lakh. The bank and the housing finance company with privately placed debentures are exempt from both.

slides.narration: Keep the two apart. The reserve is profit kept back, ten per cent of all outstanding debentures, shown in reserves and surplus, and moved to general reserve after redemption. The investment is money set aside, fifteen per cent of what matures this year, shown as a current investment, and encashed to pay the holders.

slides.heading: Out of capital or out of profits?

rows: A company exempt from the reserve (e.g. a listed company)
Any company; the minimum for an unlisted company
Up to the full face value to be redeemed

visual.alt: Table of the sources of redemption: out of capital with no transfer, open to a company exempt from the reserve; partly out of profits with the ten per cent minimum; wholly out of profits with a transfer up to the full face value; in both profit cases the reserve goes to general reserve after redemption

slides.narration: The source of redemption tells us how much profit is kept back first. Out of capital, none is kept back, and only a company exempt from the reserve can do this. Partly out of profits means the statutory ten per cent. Wholly out of profits means keeping back an amount equal to the full face value. Whatever is kept back goes to general reserve after redemption.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: Sarthebari weighs its choice
slides.body_md: By 1 April 2026 Sarthebari's surplus is ₹26,00,000. Compare keeping the statutory reserve with redeeming wholly out of profits.

visual.alt: Table of worked example four comparing Sarthebari's two choices with a surplus of 26,00,000: partly out of profits needs no further transfer and leaves the whole surplus; wholly out of profits needs a further 18,00,000, leaving 8,00,000; the general reserve later receives 2,00,000 or 20,00,000; the investment is 3,00,000 either way
visual.caption: Wholly out of profits: Surplus, i.e., Balance in Statement of Profit and Loss Dr. To Debenture Redemption Reserve A/c ₹18,00,000.

slides.narration: With the statutory reserve, nothing more is transferred and the whole surplus stays available for dividend. Wholly out of profits, a further rupees eighteen lakh goes to the reserve, leaving only rupees eight lakh. In both cases the investment is rupees three lakh, and the reserve later becomes general reserve.

slides.narration: For the same debentures, the three sources keep back very different amounts of profit. Out of capital keeps back nothing. Partly out of profits keeps back the statutory tenth. Wholly out of profits keeps back the full face value, so resources equal to the whole debt stay in the business after the holders are paid.

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the reserve comes out of profits available for dividend and is used only for redemption; ten per cent for unlisted companies; fifteen per cent investment by the thirtieth of April for listed and other unlisted companies; out of capital means no transfer; out of profits means the ten per cent or the full face value, later moved to general reserve

slides.narration: To sum up: the reserve comes out of profits available for dividend and is used only for redemption. Ordinary unlisted companies keep ten per cent. Listed and ordinary unlisted companies invest fifteen per cent of debentures maturing in the year by the thirtieth of April. Out of capital means no transfer; out of profits means the tenth or the full face value.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Classify the company **first** (listed, unlisted, bank, NBFC or HFC): the rule follows from the class.
Reserve = 10% of **outstanding** debentures; investment = 15% of debentures **maturing in the year**.
Debit **Surplus** (not Bank) for the reserve; debit the **investment** and credit Bank when money is set aside.
Wholly out of profits: transfer the **face value less the reserve already held**.
Write the working for every percentage: it carries a step mark.
slides.narration: Start by classifying the company, because the rules follow from its class. Take ten per cent of outstanding debentures for the reserve, and fifteen per cent of those maturing this year for the investment. Debit the surplus for the reserve, but credit the bank when the investment is made. When redeeming wholly out of profits, transfer only what the reserve still lacks. And always show your working.

nodes.label: Before redemption: top up the reserve (Surplus → Debenture Redemption Reserve)
By 30 April: invest 15% (Debenture Redemption Investment ← Bank)
On maturity: encash the investment with interest

visual.alt: Flow of a lump-sum redemption: top up the reserve, invest fifteen per cent by the thirtieth of April, encash it with interest on maturity, transfer the debentures and any premium to the debentureholders and pay them, then move the reserve to general reserve and the interest to the statement of profit and loss
visual.caption: Lump-sum redemption, step by step

slides.narration: A lump-sum redemption follows a set order. First the reserve is topped up from the surplus. By the thirtieth of April the fifteen per cent investment is made. On maturity the investment is encashed with interest, the debentures are transferred to the holders account, and the holders are paid. Finally the reserve goes to general reserve, and the interest is closed to profit and loss.

sections.heading: 1. Redemption: meaning, methods and sources
sections.body_md:
**Redemption** of debentures is the repayment of the amount due to the debentureholders, which discharges the company's liability.

- **Methods in the ISC 2027 syllabus:** (a) in **one lump sum** at the end of the stated period, at par or at a premium; (b) in **annual instalments by draw of lots** (concepts only).
- **Sources:** out of **capital** (no profit kept back), **partly out of profits** (the statutory reserve) or **wholly out of profits** (a reserve equal to the face value redeemed).
- **Safeguards:** the **Debenture Redemption Reserve** (profit kept back) and the **Debenture Redemption Investment** (money set aside).

Not in the ISC 2027 syllabus: calculation of ex-interest and cum-interest prices, and numerical problems on redemption by draw of lots.

sections.heading: 2. Debenture Redemption Reserve: who and how much
sections.body_md:
**Section 71(4), Companies Act, 2013:** a company issuing debentures creates a Debenture Redemption Reserve **out of profits available for payment of dividend**; the amount credited may be used **only for redeeming debentures**.

**Rule 18(7), as amended in 2019:**
- **Other unlisted companies:** reserve of at least **10% of the value of outstanding debentures**.
- **Not required:** listed companies; All India Financial Institutions and banking companies; unlisted NBFCs and housing finance companies (HFCs) for privately placed debentures.

**Entry:** Surplus, i.e., Balance in Statement of Profit and Loss Dr. To Debenture Redemption Reserve A/c.

**Further transfer** = 10% × outstanding debentures − balance already in the reserve (nil if already enough).

sections.heading: 3. Debenture Redemption Investment
sections.body_md:
**Rule 18(7):** on or before **30 April** each year, a listed company or an unlisted company (other than the exempt classes) must invest or deposit at least **15% of the debentures maturing during the year ending on the next 31 March**.

- **Permitted forms:** deposits with a scheduled bank free from any charge or lien; unencumbered securities of the Central or a State Government; unencumbered trust securities and notified bonds under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882.
- **Use:** only for redeeming the debentures maturing that year; it must never fall below 15% of them.

**Entries:** made: Debenture Redemption Investment A/c Dr. To Bank A/c; encashed: Bank A/c Dr. To Debenture Redemption Investment A/c, Interest on Debenture Redemption Investment A/c; interest closed: Interest on Debenture Redemption Investment A/c Dr. To Statement of Profit and Loss.

sections.heading: 5. Redemption out of profits and out of capital
sections.body_md:
- **Out of capital:** no profit is transferred to a reserve; the funds paid out are not replaced by retained profit. Open only to a company exempt from the reserve (for example a listed company, which still makes the 15% investment).
- **Partly out of profits:** the statutory reserve (10% of outstanding debentures) is kept; after redemption it goes to General Reserve.
- **Wholly out of profits:** an amount equal to the **face value redeemed** is kept in the reserve before redemption: further transfer = face value − reserve already held. After redemption it goes to General Reserve, so resources equal to the debt repaid stay in the business.

**Entries:** Surplus, i.e., Balance in Statement of Profit and Loss Dr. To Debenture Redemption Reserve A/c (before); Debenture Redemption Reserve A/c Dr. To General Reserve A/c (after).

sections.heading: 6. Redemption in a lump sum at par
sections.body_md:
**Order of entries for the year of redemption**
1. Transfer to reserve (if it is short of the minimum).
2. Investment made by 30 April.
3. Investment encashed with interest on maturity.
4. Debentures A/c Dr. To Debentureholders' A/c (amount due).
5. Debentureholders' A/c Dr. To Bank A/c (payment).
6. Debenture Redemption Reserve A/c Dr. To General Reserve A/c.
7. Interest on the investment closed to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

**Check:** Debentures, Debentureholders, the investment and the reserve all close at **nil**; the bank changes by interest earned − amount repaid.

sections.heading: 8. Redemption in instalments by draw of lots (concepts only)
sections.body_md:
- A fixed part of the issue is redeemed each year; the debenture numbers to be repaid are chosen by **draw of lots**.
- Holders whose debentures are drawn are repaid **in full**; the rest continue to earn interest until drawn.
- **Reserve:** the 10% minimum is built before redemption begins and transferred to General Reserve after the last instalment.
- **Investment:** by 30 April of each year, at least **15% of that year’s instalment** is invested; it is encashed for that instalment and made again for the next.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Debiting **Bank** instead of the surplus when creating the reserve.
- Taking 15% of **all** debentures for the investment: it is 15% of those **maturing in the year**.
- Asking a **listed** company for a reserve (none since 2019), or forgetting that it still makes the **investment**.
- Transferring the reserve to **Capital Reserve** after redemption; it goes to **General Reserve**.
- Debiting the Debentures Account straight to Bank, skipping the **Debentureholders' Account**.
- Charging the premium on redemption to profit at maturity; it was provided for **at issue**.
- Treating interest on the investment as part of the investment; it is **income**.

**How marks are usually awarded (SOYL chapter tests on the ISC default pattern)**
- 1 mark: objective items.
- 2 marks: one or two entries with the working, or two points of difference.
- 3 marks: a set of redemption entries, a ledger account or a comparison table.
- 5 marks in parts, e.g. (a) 3 + (b) 2: entries for the year and the ledger accounts or an explanation.
- Full practical (practice, 8 marks): entries about 5, ledger accounts or notes about 3. The ISC 2027 weightage for Issue and Redemption of Debentures in Paper I is 8 marks.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: Srikalahasti Kalamkari Ltd, an imagined unlisted company, will redeem its debentures in four annual instalments by draw of lots. Explain how its Debenture Redemption Reserve and its Debenture Redemption Investment are handled during these four years.
questions.solution_md: Separate the reserve, kept once and released at the end, from the investment, which is made and used again for each instalment.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Reserve:** before redemption begins, the company builds up at least 10% of the outstanding debentures in the Debenture Redemption Reserve out of profits available for dividend. The reserve can be used only for redemption; once the last instalment has been paid, it is transferred to General Reserve.

2. **Investment, renewed every year:** by 30 April of each year the company invests or deposits at least 15% of the instalment maturing in that year, in a permitted form free from charge.

3. **Use of the investment:** when that year’s instalment falls due, the investment is encashed and used towards paying the holders drawn; a fresh investment is then made for the next instalment, so it never falls below 15% of the debentures maturing in the year.

marking_scheme.step: Reserve: 10% out of profits, used only for redemption, to General Reserve at the end
Investment: 15% of the instalment maturing each year, by 30 April
Investment encashed for each instalment and renewed for the next

(b) Explain how the company would meet the Debenture Redemption Reserve and Debenture Redemption Investment rules under each choice. [3]
questions.solution_md: The reserve rule is the same; the investment follows what matures in each year, so it is made once for a lump sum and every year for instalments.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Each year a fixed part of the issue is repaid. The debentures to be repaid are chosen by a random draw, and their holders are repaid in full; the rest continue to earn interest until drawn. **Advantage:** the cash outflow is spread over several years instead of one large payment, and interest falls as the outstanding debentures fall.

**(b)**
- **Reserve (both choices):** as an unlisted company it builds the reserve to at least 10% of the outstanding debentures out of profits before redemption begins, and moves it to General Reserve after the last repayment.
- **Investment, lump sum:** by 30 April of the year of maturity it invests at least 15% of the whole issue, and encashes it on the redemption date.
- **Investment, instalments:** by 30 April of each year of redemption it invests at least 15% of that year’s instalment, uses it towards that instalment, and repeats for the next one.
